item.title: Sitting down to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One: - Here, venerable sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala has had many people bound.…
item.description:
Sitting down to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One:
- Here, venerable sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala has had many people bound. Some are bound with ropes, some with chains, some with shackles.

Then the Blessed One, understanding the meaning of this, on that occasion recited this verse:
The wise say that such binding
Is not strong —
Binding with iron, with ropes,
With wooden shackles —
But infatuation with sensual pleasures,
With jewels and ornaments,
And anxious thoughts
Directed toward children and wives —
The wise say this binding
Is truly strong.
Though it drags one down,
Subtle and hard to escape,
True renunciants cut it in two,
Without wishing or longing,
Abandoning all sensual pleasures.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.10

item.title: “What is wandering without a standing place? The bondage of standing and clinging to the sign of forms, householder, has been abandoned by the Tathāgata,…
item.description:
“What is wandering without a standing place? The bondage of standing and clinging to the sign of forms, householder, has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made non-existent, so that it cannot arise again in the future. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called ‘one who wanders without a standing place.’ The bondage of standing and clinging to the sign of sounds … smells … tastes … touches … phenomena, householder, has been abandoned by the Tathāgata … Therefore, the Tathāgata is called ‘one who wanders without a standing place.’ Thus, householder, is wandering without a standing place.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.3

item.title: Speak with a person Who holds a sword in hand, Speak with a demon, Or sit closely with them. A poisonous snake — If bitten,…
item.description:
Speak with a person
Who holds a sword in hand,
Speak with a demon,
Or sit closely with them.
A poisonous snake —
If bitten, one dies —
But do not alone
Speak with a woman.
Mindless, they bind one
With glances, with smiles,
With revealing clothes,
With sweet words —
Still not satisfied,
One becomes unconscious and dies.
These five strands of sensual pleasure
Are seen in female form —
Form, sound, smell, taste, touch —
Enticing and agreeable.
Overwhelmed by the waterfall of sensuality,
Flooded and swept away,
The foolish and ignorant,
Not understanding sensual pleasures.
Humans, at death,
Go to states of existence and non-existence —
They are led on
Through many births.
Those who understand sensual pleasures,
Without fear in their conduct,
Reach the far shore,
Attaining the destruction of the defilements.

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.55
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: … (At Sāvatthi). Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One: As if struck by a sword,…
item.description:
… (At Sāvatthi). Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
As if struck by a sword,
As if fire blazed on the head —
Mindful, a monk should go forth,
Abandoning lust for sensual pleasures.

(The Blessed One):
As if struck by a sword,
As if fire blazed on the head —
Mindful, a monk should go forth,
Abandoning identity view.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.21

item.title: “And how, monks, is a monk ‘knowing and understanding’? He has known and understood evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, fearful,…
item.description:
“And how, monks, is a monk ‘knowing and understanding’? He has known and understood evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, fearful, producing painful results, leading to future birth, aging, and death. Thus, monks, a monk is ‘knowing and understanding.’”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 39 – Mahāhatthipadopamasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Aggivessana, pleasant feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. Aggivessana, painful feeling is…
item.description:
“Aggivessana, pleasant feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. Aggivessana, painful feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. Aggivessana, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 74 – Dīghanakhasutta

item.title: Sitting down to one side, the Venerable Rādha said to the Blessed One: “Good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma…
item.description:
Sitting down to one side, the Venerable Rādha said to the Blessed One: “Good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief. Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I will dwell alone, secluded, heedful, ardent, and resolute.” - “Rādha, whatever is impermanent — there you should abandon your desire. And what, Rādha, is impermanent? The eye, Rādha, is impermanent — there you should abandon your desire. Forms are impermanent … Eye-consciousness … Eye-contact … Whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact — pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant — that feeling is impermanent. There you should abandon your desire. The ear … The nose … The tongue … The body … The mind is impermanent — there you should abandon your desire. Phenomena … Mind-consciousness … Mind-contact … Whatever feeling arises dependent on mind-contact — pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant — that feeling is impermanent. There you should abandon your desire. Whatever is impermanent, Rādha — there you should abandon your desire.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.76
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, one who dwells seeing danger in things that are fetters — greed is abandoned, hatred is abandoned, delusion is abandoned. Because greed, hatred, and…
item.description:
“Monks, one who dwells seeing danger in things that are fetters — greed is abandoned, hatred is abandoned, delusion is abandoned. Because greed, hatred, and delusion are abandoned, he is freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that he is freed from suffering.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.6

item.title: “Once, monks, a hawk suddenly swooped down and seized a quail. Then, monks, the quail, while being carried off by the hawk, lamented: ‘This is…
item.description:
“Once, monks, a hawk suddenly swooped down and seized a quail. Then, monks, the quail, while being carried off by the hawk, lamented: ‘This is my misfortune! This is my lack of merit! For I wandered outside my own proper range, into the domain of others. If I had kept to my own proper range, my ancestral territory, this hawk would not have been a match for me in battle.’ - ‘What, quail, is your own proper range, your ancestral territory?’ - ‘A field plowed with a plow.’ Then, monks, the hawk, not boasting of its own strength, not pressing its own strength, released the quail and said: ‘Go, quail. Even after going there, I will not let you go.’ Then, monks, the quail went to a field plowed with a plow, climbed onto a large clod of earth, stood on it, and said to the hawk: ‘Come at me, hawk! Come at me, hawk!’ Then the hawk, boasting of its own strength, pressing its own strength, folding both wings, suddenly swooped down on the quail. When the quail knew: ‘This hawk is swooping down hard on me,’ it hid behind that clod of earth. Then, monks, the hawk shattered its own breast. So too, monks, for one who wanders outside his own proper range, into the domain of others. Therefore, monks, do not wander outside your own proper range, into the domain of others. For one who wanders outside his proper range, into the domain of others, Māra gains an opportunity, Māra gains an object.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.6
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, there is no form that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain forever. There is no feeling … perception ……
item.description:
“Monks, there is no form that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain forever. There is no feeling … perception … formation … consciousness that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain forever.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.98
